name: Antegrade femoral nailing through a trochanteric entry
corridor: Proximal gluteal split aligned with the femoral bow to a centered start at the greater-trochanter tip

positioning.text: Position supine or lateral with the pelvis accessible and obtain true AP and axial/lateral images of the greater trochanter and proximal femur.

setup.text: Drape to the pelvic rim, plan reduction and traction, and verify imaging from the trochanter through the distal femur before incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the trochanter tip, femoral axis, projected bow, and pelvic rim using fluoroscopy when necessary.

incision.text: Make a 3–5 cm incision about 10–15 cm proximal to the trochanter tip, farther proximal in obesity, along the proximal extension of the femoral bow.

superficial_interval.text: Open fascia and split gluteal fibers longitudinally, maintaining a direct soft-tissue track aligned with the femoral shaft.

deep_interval.text: Palpate the trochanter and establish a guidewire start adjacent to its tip on AP view and exactly centered on the axial view.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, gluteal fascia, longitudinal gluteal split, trochanteric cortex, then femoral canal.

structures_encountered.text: Gluteal fascia and muscle, abductor insertion region, greater trochanter, proximal cortex, and femoral canal define the approach.

structures_at_risk.text: The superior gluteal nerve, abductor tissue, anterior and posterior trochanteric walls, femoral neck, and posterior shaft cortex are at risk.

danger_zones.text: An off-center axial start or distal skin portal produces anterior/posterior trochanter blowout, eccentric reaming, medial cortical weakening, or neck stress.

retraction_hazards.text: Do not lever instruments against the trochanter to compensate for a distal incision; extend proximally until the soft-tissue track is collinear.

exposure.text: Provides a relatively accessible start for proximally curved antegrade nails with limited fracture-site dissection.

limitations.text: The start must match nail geometry and be centered axially; a nominally easier portal does not tolerate imprecise positioning.

extensions.text: Extend the incision proximally for collinearity or add a limited fracture reduction window if closed reduction fails.

indications.text: Use for selected shaft and distal-third fractures treated with a compatible proximally curved antegrade nail.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose another portal or strategy when proximal anatomy, previous implants, abductor pathology, habitus, or nail design prevents a safe centered start.

implant_implications.text: Use a nail specifically designed for trochanteric entry and keep wire, opening reamer, and nail centered through the trochanter into the canal.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Verify the start on AP and axial/lateral views, then monitor centered reaming, fracture alignment, nail depth, and locking.

closure.text: Irrigate, repair fascia without abductor tethering, and close subcutaneous tissue and skin.

complications.text: Complications include abductor injury and hip pain, trochanteric blowout, femoral-neck stress fracture, cortical perforation, malalignment, nonunion, and infection.

bailouts.text: If a centered track cannot be established, stop repeated opening attempts, reposition or extend the exposure, or change to another compatible nailing strategy.

procedure_applications.condition: A proximally curved antegrade nail is selected and a centered greater-trochanter start matches implant design

questions.question: Where must the trochanteric start lie on axial imaging?
questions.answer: Exactly centered on the greater trochanter and aligned with the canal.

questions.question: Which nail geometry uses this portal?
questions.answer: A proximally curved antegrade nail designed for trochanteric entry.

questions.question: What can an eccentric start cause?
questions.answer: Trochanteric wall blowout, eccentric reaming, malalignment, or femoral-neck stress.
